papers.full_text: Can Hantavirus cruise into the next pandemic? Despite concerns arising from a recent ship-associated outbreak on the M/V Hondius cruise, current evidence suggests that Andes virus (ANDV) poses a low pandemic risk. Nevertheless, viral evolution, ecological changes, and reservoir host dynamics could drive future emergence of ANDV, underscoring the need for improved surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccine preparedness. Hantaviruses are part of the family Hantaviridae, which comprises eight genera. Among them, viruses associated with human disease belong to the genus Orthohantavirus. Orthohantaviruses are enveloped, tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA viruses whose genome consists of small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments encoding the nucleocapsid protein (N), glycoproteins Gn/Gc, and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), respectively. The two major clinical diseases caused by orthohantaviruses are haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome/cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS). HFRS is mainly caused by Asian and European orthohantaviruses, including Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, and Dobrava virus, and primarily affects the kidneys. In contrast, HPS/HCPS is caused by several American orthohantaviruses, including Orthohantavirus sinnonbrenense (Sin Nombre virus; SNV) and Orthohantavirus andesense (Andes virus; ANDV), and is characterised by severe respiratory disease, pulmonary oedema, and cardiovascular compromise. Importantly, ANDV-associated HPS is characterised by high case-fatality rates, with mortality estimates in Chile and Argentina ranging from approximately 21% to 50%. Orthohantavirus infection is primarily acquired by inhaling aerosolised particles contaminated with the urine, saliva, or faeces of infected rodents, although transmission may also occur through direct contact with contaminated materials or rodent bites. While most orthohantaviruses are transmitted exclusively from rodents to humans, ANDV is unique among orthohantaviruses for its demonstrated capacity for person-to-person transmission, particularly during close, prolonged contact with symptomatic individuals. Although sustained community transmission has not been demonstrated, ANDV remains the only orthohantavirus for which person-to-person transmission has been consistently documented, predominantly among close household or intimate contacts. On 4 May 2026, an international cluster of ANDV infections was identified among passengers travelling aboard the M/V Hondius following its departure from Ushuaia, Argentina. The event prompted a multinational public health response involving case isolation, quarantine, surveillance, contact tracing, and genomic investigation. The WHO declared the outbreak over on 2 July 2026, with 13 cases reported, including 3 fatalities. The M/V Hondius cluster therefore provides an important contemporary example of ANDV’s epidemic potential. Could ANDV cause a future pandemic? Despite documented person-to-person transmission associated with the M/V Hondius cluster, current epidemiological and genomic evidence indicates that the likelihood of this outbreak progressing to sustained epidemic or pandemic transmission was exceedingly low. Prompt implementation of public health interventions, including quarantine measures and active surveillance of individuals aboard the vessel, facilitated the early identification and isolation of suspected cases. Furthermore, genomic analyses revealed remarkably limited viral diversity among sequenced cases from the M/V Hondius cluster, with identical S and M segment sequences and only two synonymous single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) detected within the L segment, one in case 5 and another in case 7. Importantly, no evidence of amino acid changes associated with enhanced transmissibility or sustained human-to-human spread was identified. In contrast, the outbreak sequences showed approximately 98.7% nucleotide identity across all three genome segments with ANDV sequences identified in Argentina in 1997 and 2018, indicating considerably greater divergence from these historical reference sequences. Furthermore, the reported positive cases fell within the incubation period of nine to 45 days for ANDV, suggesting that the cluster may have originated from a limited zoonotic exposure event, potentially followed by restricted secondary transmission, and is unlikely to develop into an epidemic or a pandemic event. However, given that ANDV has historically caused multiple outbreaks, it is important to highlight the conditions that could enable localised ANDV outbreaks to evolve and escalate into larger epidemics, and potentially, under exceptional circumstances, into a pandemic threat among human populations, as illustrated in Figure. Potential drivers of Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak escalation and pandemic emergence. ANDV is maintained in rodent reservoirs, primarily the long-tailed pygmy rice rat (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus), and is transmitted to humans through inhalation of aerosolised rodent excreta. Unlike other orthohantaviruses, ANDV can also undergo limited person-to-person transmission, although sustained community transmission has not been documented. The graphical abstract highlights three factors that could contribute to outbreak escalation: (i) viral evolution through mutation, reassortment, and host adaptation; (ii) environmental and ecological changes that increase rodent abundance and spillover risk; and (iii) expansion of reservoir host range through host switching and reservoir diversification. Under favourable ecological and evolutionary conditions, these processes could increase the scale, frequency, geographic distribution, or transmission potential of future outbreaks, underscoring the importance of continued surveillance, preparedness, and the development of effective diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccines. Illustration created with BioRender.com. First - The acquisition of beneficial mutations may facilitate adaptation to human hosts. Genetic variation arising during viral replication could theoretically influence viral fitness, host range, or transmission efficiency under selective pressures. Orthohantaviruses replicate using an error-prone RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), with evolutionary rates estimated at approximately 10−2-10−4 substitutions per site per year, consistent with rates reported for other RNA viruses. However, the relationship between genomic variation and altered transmissibility in ANDV remains incompletely understood, and no specific adaptive mutations have yet been conclusively associated with sustained human-to-human transmission. Previous studies have shown that ANDV strains from rodent and human hosts can produce markedly different outcomes in the Syrian hamster model. Notably, a Chilean human isolate (CHI-7913), recovered from a fatal HPS case, acquired only a single non-synonymous mutation after 25 serial passages in hamsters and remained non-pathogenic, indicating relative genomic stability. In contrast, the rodent-derived isolate Chile-9717869 causes uniformly lethal disease despite differing by 23 amino acids from CHI-7913. Although these findings suggest a degree of genomic stability, they do not necessarily preclude adaptation. One possible explanation is that the CHI-7913 isolate had already undergone host-specific adaptation following zoonotic transmission to humans, thereby enhancing fitness in human cells while reducing replication efficiency and pathogenicity in the Syrian hamster model. Collectively, these observations indicate that relatively few genetic changes can substantially alter host adaptation and disease phenotype in ANDV, while the molecular determinants governing virulence and transmissibility remain incompletely understood. Several biological mechanisms may contribute to these processes, including alterations in receptor usage, interferon antagonism, and genome reassortment. Pathogenic orthohantaviruses utilise β3 integrins, protocadherin-1, and other endothelium-associated receptors for host-cell entry, and mutations affecting glycoprotein-receptor interactions could alter host permissiveness and enhance adaptation to humans. In addition, the ability of orthohantaviruses to suppress interferon signalling contributes to reservoir persistence and may influence pathogenicity across different hosts. Importantly, the segmented orthohantavirus genome permits genetic reassortment during co-infection, potentially generating novel phenotypic combinations with altered virulence, transmissibility, or host range. Although reassortment appears less frequent than in other members of the order Bunyavirales (e.g. orthobunyaviruses) and influenza viruses, it remains an important mechanism contributing to long-term evolutionary adaptation and host expansion. Second - An increase in rodent reservoir populations driven by environmental and ecological changes may amplify the risk of zoonotic spillover. Environmental disruption is a well-recognised determinant of orthohantavirus emergence and transmission dynamics. Climatic oscillations, including El Niño-associated rainfall patterns, can substantially increase rodent abundance and population density, thereby elevating opportunities for human exposure, as previously documented during Sin Nombre virus (SNV) outbreaks in North America. In South America, deforestation, agricultural expansion, urban encroachment into rural and forested ecosystems, and biodiversity disturbance may similarly intensify contact between humans and ANDV reservoir hosts. In parallel, globalisation and expanding transportation networks have facilitated the international dissemination of rodent-associated orthohantaviruses, as illustrated by the spread of Seoul virus (SEOV) through maritime trade and the pet rat industry. Collectively, these ecological and anthropogenic pressures may increase the frequency of spillover events and the geographic distribution of orthohantavirus exposure. However, there is currently no evidence that such conditions alone are sufficient to drive sustained human-to-human transmission or pandemic-level spread of ANDV. Third - Expansion of reservoir host range may contribute to broader geographic dissemination and increased opportunities for human exposure. Orthohantaviruses were historically considered highly host-specific pathogens, with individual virus lineages predominantly associated with a single rodent reservoir species through long-term co-evolutionary relationships. ANDV is primarily associated with Oligoryzomys longicaudatus as its principal reservoir host. However, accumulating phylogenetic and ecological evidence has challenged the concept of strict host specificity, demonstrating that host-switching events, spillover infections, and reservoir diversification have likely occurred repeatedly throughout orthohantavirus evolutionary history. In addition, the identification of genetically divergent orthohantaviruses in shrews, moles, and bats suggests that ancestral orthohantaviruses may have undergone multiple historical cross-species transmission events. Collectively, these findings indicate that orthohantavirus host associations, although generally stable, are not biologically absolute. Habitat disruptions, altered species interactions, and environmental pressures could therefore increase opportunities for cross-species transmission and geographic expansion over extended ecological timescales, potentially increasing the frequency of human exposure to infected reservoir hosts. Nevertheless, there is currently no evidence that such ecological processes have resulted in ANDV lineages with enhanced sustained human-to-human transmissibility. Current preparedness against ANDV outbreaks Perhaps more worrying is the limited availability of rapid diagnostics, antivirals, and vaccines for responding to outbreaks of ANDV and other clinically relevant orthohantaviruses. Several antiviral and immunotherapeutic strategies have been explored against human disease-causing orthohantaviruses, including nucleoside analogues such as ribavirin, favipiravir and ETAR; entry inhibitors such as lactoferrin and griffithsin; host-directed approaches targeting vascular leakage pathways; RNAi-based strategies; and, more recently, neutralising monoclonal antibodies targeting the Gn/Gc glycoprotein complex. However, no orthohantavirus-specific antiviral has yet become an established standard of care, and most candidates remain experimental or dependent on very early administration. In parallel, vaccine development efforts have advanced substantially over the past decades. Hantavax®, an inactivated orthohantavirus vaccine marketed in South Korea to prevent HFRS caused by Hantaan and Seoul viruses, remains among the only orthohantavirus vaccines licensed for human use, while several next-generation vaccine candidates are currently under development and evaluation in preclinical and early-phase clinical trials. Despite these advances, effective countermeasures specifically targeting ANDV remain limited, highlighting an important preparedness gap for future outbreaks. In conclusion - Overall, current evidence does not support the conclusion that ANDV is imminently poised to emerge as a pandemic pathogen comparable to severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). Nevertheless, under favourable ecological and epidemiological conditions, localised ANDV outbreaks may increase in scale or geographic distribution, potentially posing broader regional public health challenges. These considerations underscore the importance of strengthening preparedness strategies to prevent the escalation of orthohantavirus outbreaks, particularly in under-resourced endemic regions of South America. Integrated ecological surveillance approaches, including climate-informed forecasting of rodent population dynamics, together with genomic epidemiological surveillance of ANDV and other clinically relevant orthohantaviruses, may improve early detection of spillover risk, characterise orthohantavirus diversity and evolutionary dynamics, and support timely public health responses. In addition, expanded availability of antiviral therapeutics, monoclonal antibodies, preventive vaccines, and rapid diagnostic platforms will be important for comprehensive orthohantavirus outbreak preparedness and response. These diagnostic platforms could include lateral-flow assays to detect orthohantavirus-specific IgM and IgG antibodies in symptomatic patients, as well as antigen-based tests for direct virus detection in both humans and reservoir hosts. full_text_sections.full_text: Can Hantavirus cruise into the next pandemic? Despite concerns arising from a recent ship-associated outbreak on the M/V Hondius cruise, current evidence suggests that Andes virus (ANDV) poses a low pandemic risk. Nevertheless, viral evolution, ecological changes, and reservoir host dynamics could drive future emergence of ANDV, underscoring the need for improved surveillance, diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccine preparedness. Hantaviruses are part of the family Hantaviridae, which comprises eight genera. Among them, viruses associated with human disease belong to the genus Orthohantavirus. Orthohantaviruses are enveloped, tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA viruses whose genome consists of small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments encoding the nucleocapsid protein (N), glycoproteins Gn/Gc, and the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), respectively. The two major clinical diseases caused by orthohantaviruses are haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome/cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS/HCPS). HFRS is mainly caused by Asian and European orthohantaviruses, including Hantaan virus, Seoul virus, Puumala virus, and Dobrava virus, and primarily affects the kidneys. In contrast, HPS/HCPS is caused by several American orthohantaviruses, including Orthohantavirus sinnonbrenense (Sin Nombre virus; SNV) and Orthohantavirus andesense (Andes virus; ANDV), and is characterised by severe respiratory disease, pulmonary oedema, and cardiovascular compromise. Importantly, ANDV-associated HPS is characterised by high case-fatality rates, with mortality estimates in Chile and Argentina ranging from approximately 21% to 50%. Orthohantavirus infection is primarily acquired by inhaling aerosolised particles contaminated with the urine, saliva, or faeces of infected rodents, although transmission may also occur through direct contact with contaminated materials or rodent bites. While most orthohantaviruses are transmitted exclusively from rodents to humans, ANDV is unique among orthohantaviruses for its demonstrated capacity for person-to-person transmission, particularly during close, prolonged contact with symptomatic individuals. Although sustained community transmission has not been demonstrated, ANDV remains the only orthohantavirus for which person-to-person transmission has been consistently documented, predominantly among close household or intimate contacts. On 4 May 2026, an international cluster of ANDV infections was identified among passengers travelling aboard the M/V Hondius following its departure from Ushuaia, Argentina. The event prompted a multinational public health response involving case isolation, quarantine, surveillance, contact tracing, and genomic investigation. The WHO declared the outbreak over on 2 July 2026, with 13 cases reported, including 3 fatalities. The M/V Hondius cluster therefore provides an important contemporary example of ANDV’s epidemic potential. Could ANDV cause a future pandemic? Despite documented person-to-person transmission associated with the M/V Hondius cluster, current epidemiological and genomic evidence indicates that the likelihood of this outbreak progressing to sustained epidemic or pandemic transmission was exceedingly low. Prompt implementation of public health interventions, including quarantine measures and active surveillance of individuals aboard the vessel, facilitated the early identification and isolation of suspected cases. Furthermore, genomic analyses revealed remarkably limited viral diversity among sequenced cases from the M/V Hondius cluster, with identical S and M segment sequences and only two synonymous single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) detected within the L segment, one in case 5 and another in case 7. Importantly, no evidence of amino acid changes associated with enhanced transmissibility or sustained human-to-human spread was identified. In contrast, the outbreak sequences showed approximately 98.7% nucleotide identity across all three genome segments with ANDV sequences identified in Argentina in 1997 and 2018, indicating considerably greater divergence from these historical reference sequences. Furthermore, the reported positive cases fell within the incubation period of nine to 45 days for ANDV, suggesting that the cluster may have originated from a limited zoonotic exposure event, potentially followed by restricted secondary transmission, and is unlikely to develop into an epidemic or a pandemic event. However, given that ANDV has historically caused multiple outbreaks, it is important to highlight the conditions that could enable localised ANDV outbreaks to evolve and escalate into larger epidemics, and potentially, under exceptional circumstances, into a pandemic threat among human populations, as illustrated in Figure. Potential drivers of Andes virus (ANDV) outbreak escalation and pandemic emergence. ANDV is maintained in rodent reservoirs, primarily the long-tailed pygmy rice rat (Oligoryzomys longicaudatus), and is transmitted to humans through inhalation of aerosolised rodent excreta. Unlike other orthohantaviruses, ANDV can also undergo limited person-to-person transmission, although sustained community transmission has not been documented. The graphical abstract highlights three factors that could contribute to outbreak escalation: (i) viral evolution through mutation, reassortment, and host adaptation; (ii) environmental and ecological changes that increase rodent abundance and spillover risk; and (iii) expansion of reservoir host range through host switching and reservoir diversification. Under favourable ecological and evolutionary conditions, these processes could increase the scale, frequency, geographic distribution, or transmission potential of future outbreaks, underscoring the importance of continued surveillance, preparedness, and the development of effective diagnostics, therapeutics, and vaccines. Illustration created with BioRender.com. First - The acquisition of beneficial mutations may facilitate adaptation to human hosts. Genetic variation arising during viral replication could theoretically influence viral fitness, host range, or transmission efficiency under selective pressures. Orthohantaviruses replicate using an error-prone RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), with evolutionary rates estimated at approximately 10−2-10−4 substitutions per site per year, consistent with rates reported for other RNA viruses. However, the relationship between genomic variation and altered transmissibility in ANDV remains incompletely understood, and no specific adaptive mutations have yet been conclusively associated with sustained human-to-human transmission. Previous studies have shown that ANDV strains from rodent and human hosts can produce markedly different outcomes in the Syrian hamster model. Notably, a Chilean human isolate (CHI-7913), recovered from a fatal HPS case, acquired only a single non-synonymous mutation after 25 serial passages in hamsters and remained non-pathogenic, indicating relative genomic stability. In contrast, the rodent-derived isolate Chile-9717869 causes uniformly lethal disease despite differing by 23 amino acids from CHI-7913. Although these findings suggest a degree of genomic stability, they do not necessarily preclude adaptation. One possible explanation is that the CHI-7913 isolate had already undergone host-specific adaptation following zoonotic transmission to humans, thereby enhancing fitness in human cells while reducing replication efficiency and pathogenicity in the Syrian hamster model. Collectively, these observations indicate that relatively few genetic changes can substantially alter host adaptation and disease phenotype in ANDV, while the molecular determinants governing virulence and transmissibility remain incompletely understood. papers.title: Development of a rapid RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b assay for dual detection of Hantaan virus and Seoul virus.
papers.abstract: Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the primary causative agents of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), presenting a persistent challenge to global public health. Prompt and precise diagnostic tools are essential for clinical investigation and the containment of HFRS outbreaks. Leveraging the programmable precision of CRISPR/Cas12b system, which has significantly advanced the field of molecular diagnostics, we developed a rapid, high-sensitivity assay for the dual detection of HTNV and SEOV. Each virus was detected in a separate, target-specific single-tube reaction. The assay combines recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with CRISPR/Cas12b-mediated fluorescence detection and uses virus-specific sgRNAs and RPA primers targeting conserved genomic regions. Using recombinant plasmid standards, both targets were detected at 1 × 10 1 copies/test in three technical replicates; this is a preliminary analytical detection threshold and does not incorporate extraction losses or matrix-associated inhibition. No cross-reactivity was observed within the evaluated four-organism non-target panel. In a preliminary feasibility assessment, all nine RT-qPCR-positive rodent samples (seven HTNV and two SEOV) were positive by the RPA-CRISPR/Cas12b assay, indicating complete positive agreement in this all-positive sample set. Because no negative samples were included, negative agreement, diagnostic specificity, false-positive rate, and overall clinical diagnostic accuracy could not be assessed. These results support further development of the assay as a potential screening tool; larger studies using well-characterized positive and negative clinical or field specimens are required.

analysis.background: Hantaan virus (HTNV) and Seoul virus (SEOV) are the primary causative agents of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), presenting a persistent challenge to global public health.
analysis.methods: The authors combined recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with CRISPR/Cas12b‑mediated fluorescence detection using virus‑specific sgRNAs and primers targeting conserved genomic regions; analytical sensitivity was assessed with recombinant plasmid standards (detecting 1 × 10¹ copies/test) and feasibility was evaluated on nine RT‑qPCR‑positive rodent samples in separate single‑tube reactions.
analysis.results: Both HTNV and SEOV were detected at 1 × 10¹ copies/test, no cross‑reactivity was observed with a four‑organism non‑target panel, and all nine RT‑qPCR‑positive rodent specimens yielded positive results; negative agreement and specificity could not be determined.
analysis.contribution: The study provides a rapid, high‑sensitivity dual‑detection assay that could serve as a screening tool for HFRS agents, leveraging CRISPR/Cas12b technology.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HTNV and SEOV cause HFRS, a global health challenge. Methods: A rapid RPA‑CRISPR/Cas12b fluorescence assay using virus‑specific sgRNAs and primers was evaluated with recombinant plasmid standards (10 copies/test) and nine RT‑qPCR‑positive rodent samples in single‑tube reactions. Results: The assay detected both viruses at 10 copies/test, showed no cross‑reactivity, and was positive for all nine rodent samples; negative performance was not assessed. Contribution: This high‑sensitivity dual‑detection platform could be a rapid screening tool for HFRS. analysis_zh.background: 汉滩病毒(HTNV)和首尔病毒(SEOV)是 肾综合征出血热(肾综合征出血热)的主要致病因子,对全球公共卫生构成持续挑战。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者将重组酶聚合酶扩增(RPA)与CRISPR/Cas12b介导的荧光检测相结合,使用针对保守基因组区域的病毒特异性sgRNA和引物;通过重组质粒标准评估分析灵敏度(检测 1 × 101 拷贝/检测),并在九个RT‐qPCR阳性的啮齿动物样本中以单管分离反应评估可行性。

papers.title: Design and in silico evaluation of PV-GNProtecta: an mRNA multi-epitope vaccine candidate against Puumala virus using immunoinformatics and structural analysis.
papers.abstract: Puumala virus (PUUV), the principal causative agent of nephropathia epidemica (NE), poses a significant public health threat due to its zoonotic transmission, renal complications, and the lack of an approved vaccine. In this study, an immunoinformatics-driven mRNA multi-epitope vaccine, PV-GNProtecta, was designed using conserved regions of the viral glycoprotein (G) and nucleoprotein (N). Highly antigenic, non-allergenic, and non-toxic T-cell and B-cell epitopes were identified and assembled with appropriate adjuvants to enhance immunogenicity. Population coverage analysis suggested broad HLA responsiveness across diverse populations. The vaccine construct exhibited favorable physicochemical properties, including stability, solubility, and antigenicity. Structural validation predicted high model quality, with 95.5% of residues located in favored Ramachandran regions and an ERRAT score of 91.4. Molecular docking and MM-GBSA analyses predicted favorable computational interactions between PV-GNProtecta and TLR4, while a 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation provided computational insights into the dynamic behavior of the vaccine-TLR4 complex. Codon optimization suggested compatibility of the designed sequence with an Escherichia coli-based expression framework. Immune simulation predicted potential humoral and cellular immune response patterns, including changes in IgG, IFN-γ, and IL-2 levels. The designed mRNA sequence exhibited favorable predicted secondary structural characteristics; however, further experimental evaluation is required to assess translational efficiency and stability. Although this study is limited to computational analyses and requires experimental validation, the findings suggest that PV-GNProtecta may represent a potential candidate for further investigation against PUUV infection.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Puumala virus (PUUV) causes nephropathia epidemica and lacks an approved vaccine, posing a public health threat. Methods: An immunoinformatics-driven approach was used to design an mRNA multi-epitope vaccine (PV-GNProtecta) from conserved glycoprotein and nucleoprotein regions, with identified non-allergenic, non-toxic T- and B-cell epitopes assembled with adjuvants and evaluated for population HLA coverage. Results: The construct displayed favorable physicochemical properties, 95.5% of residues in favored Ramachandran regions, ERRAT score 91.4, strong predicted interactions with TLR4, 100 ns MD simulation stability, codon optimization compatible with E. coli, and immune simulation indicated increased IgG, IFN‑γ, IL‑2. Limitations: The work is limited to in silico analyses and requires experimental validation to confirm translational efficiency, stability, and immunogenicity.

papers.title_zh: 设计并进行计算评估 PV‐GNProtecta:一种针对 普马拉病毒 的 mRNA 多表位疫苗候选,采用免疫信息学和结构分析

analysis_zh.background: 普马拉病毒 (PUUV) 引起流行性肾病,且尚无获批疫苗,构成公共卫生威胁。
analysis_zh.methods: 采用免疫信息学驱动的方法,从保守的糖蛋白和核蛋白区域设计了 mRNA 多表位疫苗 (PV‐GNProtecta),筛选出无致敏性、无毒性的 T 细胞和 B 细胞表位,结合佐剂组装,并评估了对人群 HLA 的覆盖率。
analysis_zh.results: 该构建体表现出良好的理化特性,95.5% 的残基位于有利的 Ramachandran 区域,ERRAT 得分 91.4,预测与 TLR4 形成强相互作用,100 ns 分子动力学模拟显示稳定,密码子优化适用于大肠杆菌,免疫模拟结果显示 IgG、IFN‐γ、IL‐2 增加。
analysis_zh.contribution: 本研究提供了经计算验证的疫苗候选方案,可为今后针对 PUUV 的实验工作提供指导。
analysis_zh.limitations: 本工作仅限于体外计算分析,需通过实验验证以确认翻译效率、稳定性和免疫原性。

papers.title: Rising spillover risk: Lessons from the Andes hantavirus outbreak.
papers.abstract: The unprecedented expansion of human activity boundaries is turning spillover from a chance event into a foreseeable ecological and epidemiological certainty. Using the 2026 Andes hantavirus cruise ship outbreak as an entry point, this study examines it within a broader driver framework: nearly all emerging infectious disease events in humans in recent decades have originated from wildlife transmission; under climate-change and land-use scenarios, approximately 3139 mammal species are projected to aggregate in new combinations by 2070, causing an estimated 4000 cross-species viral transmission events. The rapid expansion of tourism into ecologically fragile regions - sub-Antarctic waters, the deep sea, and primary forests - the persistence of habitat fragmentation and animal trade, and the reshaping of wildlife distribution and vector dynamics by extreme climate events together constitute "novel contact amplifiers" that accelerate contact at the human-animal-environment interface. Robotics, artificial intelligence, autonomous driving, and automated logistics are extending human activities into previously inaccessible regions, yet they remain almost entirely absent from current spillover risk assessments. The limitations of cruise ship medical systems - whose core capacity lies in "recognize, isolate, stabilize, and transfer" rather than definitive diagnosis and treatment - were fully exposed in this event. From a One Health perspective, this paper proposes that responses to spillover risk must shift from passive reaction to proactive interface governance, incorporate technology-driven increases in contact frequency into prevention and control frameworks, and advance cornerstone strategies such as broad-spectrum vaccines and broad-spectrum antiviral drugs at the basic research level.

papers.title: Differential PCDH1 usage by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal hantaviruses.
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus are hantaviruses associated with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), but their cellular entry receptors have not been defined. We used replication-competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing hantavirus Gn/Gc glycoprotein complexes to compare entry by these viruses, the Old World rodent-borne Dabieshan virus and Tigray virus, and the shrew-borne Cao Bang virus and Amga virus. All six Gn/Gc complexes supported infection of primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells, with virus-specific efficiencies and kinetics. Genetic ablation of protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) reduced infection mediated by Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus Gn/Gc in human osteosarcoma and endothelial cells, whereas PCDH1 re-expression restored susceptibility. Both viruses were captured by a soluble PCDH1 protein comprising the first two extracellular cadherin domains. Infection was also inhibited by a soluble decoy containing the first cadherin domain, and by an antibody specific to that domain, indicating that the first PCDH1 cadherin domain mediates viral engagement. Black Creek Canal Gn/Gc-bearing rVSVs incorporated less Gn/Gc and showed lower apparent capture by PCDH1 than Laguna Negra virus and Andes virus Gn/Gc-bearing particles, even after normalization for glycoprotein abundance. In contrast, PCDH1 depletion did not detectably alter infection mediated by the other four hantavirus Gn/Gc complexes. Thus, Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus use PCDH1 for efficient entry but differ in apparent receptor engagement and responses to PCDH1-directed inhibitors, whereas all six viruses are potently neutralized by the broadly reactive Gn/Gc-directed antibody ADI-42898. IMPORTANCE: The receptors used by many medically important hantaviruses remain incompletely characterized. Using BSL2-compatible rVSVs bearing hantavirus glycoproteins, we show that Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus, two hantaviruses associated with human cardiopulmonary disease, used protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) for efficient entry into human cells. PCDH1-directed inhibitors blocked infection, but the two viruses differed in apparent receptor engagement and inhibitor sensitivity, showing that PCDH1 usage is not uniform even among closely related viruses. Gn/Gc complexes from four additional divergent hantaviruses carried by shrews and Old World rodents infected primary human endothelial cells without detectable PCDH1 dependence, emphasizing the need to identify alternative entry factors. A broadly reactive antibody neutralized every virus in the study panel, supporting conserved viral glycoprotein surfaces as therapeutic targets when receptor usage is diverse or unknown.

analysis.background: Laguna Negra virus and Black Creek Canal virus are hantaviruses linked to hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), but their cellular entry receptors had not been defined.
analysis.methods: Replication‑competent recombinant vesicular stomatitis viruses (rVSVs) bearing hantavirus Gn/Gc glycoprotein complexes were used to compare entry into primary human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells and other human cell lines.
analysis.results: All six Gn/Gc complexes infected primary endothelial cells; genetic ablation of PCDH1 reduced infection by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal viruses, which was restored by PCDH1 re‑expression; soluble PCDH1 and an antibody to its first cadherin domain blocked entry; Black Creek Canal Gn/Gc showed lower apparent PCDH1 capture than Laguna Negra; the other four hantavirus Gn/Gc complexes were PCDH1‑independent; a broadly reactive Gn/Gc‑directed antibody neutralized every virus tested.
analysis.contribution: Demonstrates that PCDH1 mediates efficient entry of two HCPS‑associated hantaviruses, reveals heterogeneity in receptor engagement among related viruses, and identifies a conserved glycoprotein antibody target for diverse hantaviruses.
analysis.limitations: Findings are derived from in‑vitro rVSV pseudotype assays reported only in the abstract, limiting detail on experimental conditions and in‑vivo relevance.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal viruses cause HCPS but lacked defined entry receptors. Methods: rVSVs bearing hantavirus Gn/Gc were used to test entry into human pulmonary endothelial cells. Results: All six Gn/Gc complexes infected cells; PCDH1 knockout reduced infection by Laguna Negra and Black Creek Canal viruses, restored by re‑expression; soluble PCDH1 and a domain‑specific antibody blocked entry; Black Creek Canal showed lower PCDH1 capture; the other four viruses were PCDH1‑independent; a broad Gn/Gc antibody neutralized all. Contribution: Identifies PCDH1 as a receptor for two HCPS viruses, shows variability in receptor use, and highlights a conserved antibody target. Limitations: Conclusions are based on in‑vitro pseudotype assays with only abstract data available.

analysis_zh.background: Laguna Negra 病毒和 Black Creek Canal 病毒是与 汉坦病毒心肺综合征(汉坦病毒心肺综合征)相关的 汉坦病毒es,但其细胞进入受体尚未确定。
analysis_zh.methods: 携带 汉坦病毒 Gn/Gc 糖蛋白复合体的可复制重组水疱性口炎病毒(rVSV)用于比较其进入人原代肺微血管内皮细胞及其他人类细胞系的情况。
analysis_zh.results: 所有六种 Gn/Gc 复合体均感染原代内皮细胞;基因敲除 PCDH1 可降低 Laguna Negra 和 Black Creek Canal 病毒的感染率,且通过 PCDH1 重表达可恢复感染;可溶性 PCDH1 及针对其第一钙黏蛋白结构域的抗体阻断了病毒进入;Black Creek Canal 的 Gn/Gc 显示的表观 PCDH1 捕获低于 Laguna Negra;其余四种 汉坦病毒 Gn/Gc 复合体不依赖 PCDH1;一种广谱的针对 Gn/Gc 的抗体中和了所有检测的病毒。
analysis_zh.contribution: 证明 PCDH1 媒介两种与汉坦病毒心肺综合征相关的 汉坦病毒es 的高效进入,揭示相关病毒在受体利用上的异质性,并确定了针对多种 汉坦病毒es 的保守糖蛋白抗体靶点。
analysis_zh.limitations: 研究结果来源于仅在摘要中报告的体外 rVSV 假型实验,限制了对实验条件和体内相关性的细节描述。

papers.title: Blood Metabolites as Biomarkers and Metabolism Mechanism Studies of Hemorrhagic Fever With Renal Syndrome.
papers.abstract: Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) is a potentially life-threatening hantavirus zoonosis endemic to East Asia, especially China, featuring fever, hemorrhage, and acute renal injury. This study aimed to identify serum metabolic biomarkers for HFRS staging and explore impaired metabolic pathways. We performed untargeted serum metabolomic profiling via ultra-performance liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) on samples from acute-phase, convalescent HFRS patients, and healthy controls. Data from untargeted metabolomics showed that 168 metabolites were significantly altered in HFRS patients. Among these, 14 metabolites could distinguish the pairwise group comparisons (patient/NC, AP/CP, AP/NC, and CP/NC), with univariate AUCs ranging from 0.7556 to 1.000; a LASSO-based combined model yielded leave-one-out cross-validated (LOOCV) AUCs of 1.000, 0.993, and 0.840 for AP/NC, CP/NC, and AP/CP, respectively, indicating their potential to distinguish disease stages. Pathway analysis revealed significant perturbations in arginine biosynthesis, ascorbate and aldarate metabolism, and taurine and hypotaurine metabolism, indicating the importance in the metabolic dysfunction of HFRS. Metabolites within the arginine biosynthesis pathway were markedly altered and effectively differentiated acute-phase HFRS from healthy controls, suggesting their role in predicting acute disease status. Distinct serum metabolite abundance shifts can stratify HFRS stages. The 14 metabolites and their combined panels discriminated disease stages with univariate AUCs of 0.756-1.000 and leave-one-out cross-validated AUCs of 0.840-1.000, supporting serum metabolites as candidate biomarkers for distinguishing HFRS stages and providing a basis for targeted metabolomics studies of HFRS.

papers.title_zh: 血液代谢物作为生物标志物及 肾综合征出血热 的代谢机制研究。

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(HFRS)是一种潜在危及生命的汉坦病毒人畜共患病,流行于东亚,尤其是中国,表现为发热、出血和急性肾损伤。
analysis_zh.methods: 对急性期、恢复期的肾综合征出血热患者及健康对照进行非靶向血清代谢组学分析,采用超高效液相色谱-串联质谱(UPLC‐MS/MS)技术。
analysis_zh.results: 在肾综合征出血热患者中,共检测到168种代谢物显著改变;其中14种代谢物在两两组比较中能够区分,单变量AUC范围为0.7556–1.000;基于LASSO的组合模型在留一交叉验证中得到AUC分别为1.000(AP/NC),0.993(CP/NC)和0.840(AP/CP);通路分析显示精氨酸生物合成、抗坏血酸及醛糖代谢、以及牛磺酸/次牛磺酸代谢出现紊乱。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些代谢物及其组合面板构成区分肾综合征出血热疾病阶段的候选血清生物标志物,并提示可能参与肾综合征出血热发病机制的代谢通路。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要数据;样本量、受试者人口学特征以及外部验证均未在所提供的证据中报告。
